title: Why We Banned Smartphones
author: SouthGlosHead
summary: Writing pseudonymously as SouthGlosHead, an Executive Headteacher of two primary schools near Bristol recounts the year-long process that led one of his schools, Blackhorse, to ban smartphones from school grounds starting September 2025. He frames the decision through nearly two decades of headship experience watching risks escalate from minor text-message disputes to predatory strangers contacting children online and a Year 6 pupil receiving 9,000 overnight WhatsApp messages. The consultation process was deliberately staged: a police-led parent workshop on safeguarding risks, a year of newsletter updates on the research (while acknowledging the evidence base is still patchy), a parent action group to surface objections, and finally a formal survey. The two main objections - safety (how will I contact my child?) and liberty (this isn't the school's business) - were each addressed with concrete compromises: allowing 'brick' phones for children walking home alone, and clarifying the ban applies only to bringing phones into school, not to ownership. The Blackhorse survey drew a 75% turnout with 87% in favour, and the school board passed the ban unanimously; the outcome at the sister school, Emersons Green, was closer at 58-42. SouthGlosHead reports zero parent complaints since the ban was announced, only messages of thanks.
points: SouthGlosHead's escalation narrative: what began as minor text-message disputes evolved over nearly two decades of headship into cyberbullying, primary-aged children sending inappropriate images, and predatory strangers contacting children online.

The triggering incident: a Year 6 pupil's confiscated phone woke to reveal 9,000 missed overnight WhatsApp messages from the class group chat - illustrating the scale of unsupervised phone use among 10-11 year-olds.

The consultation design deliberately separated information-sharing from decision-making: a police-led safeguarding workshop and a year of newsletter updates on the research preceded any formal proposal, followed by a parent action group and then a survey.

The two main parent objections - safety (contacting a child walking home alone) and liberty (school overreach) - were addressed with specific compromises: permitting simple 'brick' phones for the commute, and clarifying the ban covers bringing phones to school, not owning one.

The result: 87% of 231 Blackhorse parents (about 75% turnout) voted in favour, the governing board passed the ban unanimously, and since the September 2025 start date the school received zero complaints and many messages of thanks.
quotes: After nearly two decades in headship, I have watched this technological phenomenon unfold slowly. At first it was imperceptible... But over the years I have seen the risks grow ever more significant and ever more frequent.
The teacher, picked up the phone, waking it, only to see a notification of 9000 missed messages from the Year 6 pupil Whatsapp group overnight. NINE THOUSAND messages in a 15 hour overnight period.
The police had far greater impact here than any educationalist. By the end there was a feeling in the room that something must be done -- although at that point we didn't know what.

The Blackhorse survey had a very high turnout (231 parents -- about 75%) and a very clear result (including from nearly all Year 5 parents whose children would be most affected) with 87% voting in favour of a ban.
Since announcing the result, I have had zero emails from parents complaining about the ban, whereas I have had a good many parents thank the school for taking a stand.
